title: Model of Cells: the Basic Unit of Life
seo_title: Secondary 1 Science: Cells Worksheets (Lower Secondary Science with Answers)
standard_code: Secondary 1: Model of Cells – the Basic Unit of Life
standard_text: Describe the functions of the parts of a typical cell, including the nucleus which contains DNA; recognise plant and animal cells as models and cells as the building blocks of tissues, organs and systems; explain division of labour at the cellular level; identify the cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, vacuole and chloroplast under a light microscope and infer whether a cell is from a plant or an animal (summary of the MOE Lower Secondary Science Syllabus).
meta_desc: Free Secondary 1 science worksheets for Singapore students on cells: parts of plant and animal cells, specialised cells, tissues and organs, and the light microscope, with answers.
key_big: The cell is the basic unit of life.
key_sub: Plant cells also have a cell wall, chloroplasts and a large vacuole.
body_html:
How to think about it

The cell is the basic unit of life. Each part of a cell has a job.

  • Nucleus: controls the cell; contains DNA. Cell membrane: controls what enters and leaves. Cytoplasm: where most reactions happen.
  • Only plant cells have a cell wall (shape and support), chloroplasts (photosynthesis) and a large central vacuole (cell sap).
  • Cells → tissues → organs → systems → organism. Specialised cells share the work: division of labour.
  • Total magnification = eyepiece × objective.
Example

A cell has a cell wall but no chloroplasts. Plant or animal?

Only plant cells have a cell wall

Answer: a plant cell, for example a root hair cell

Example

Eyepiece ×10, objective ×10. Total magnification?

Multiply, do not add

Answer: ×100

Common mistakes

  • Saying animal cells have a cell wall. Only plant cells do.
  • Mixing up the cell wall and the cell membrane. The membrane controls what goes in and out.
  • Thinking every plant cell has chloroplasts. Root cells do not.
  • Adding the eyepiece and objective magnifications instead of multiplying.

faq.q: What is the difference between a plant cell and an animal cell?
faq.a: Plant cells have a cell wall, a large central vacuole and often chloroplasts. Animal cells have none of these.
It controls the activities of the cell and contains DNA, the genetic material.

faq.q: How do you work out total magnification?
faq.a: Multiply the eyepiece magnification by the objective magnification.

items.q: Where is the nucleus found: in animal cells, plant cells or both?
items.e: Plant cells have everything animal cells have, plus a cell wall, chloroplasts and a large vacuole.

items.q: Where are the chloroplasts found: in animal cells, plant cells or both?
items.e: Plant cells have everything animal cells have, plus a cell wall, chloroplasts and a large vacuole.

items.q: Where is a large permanent vacuole found: in animal cells, plant cells or both?
items.e: Plant cells have everything animal cells have, plus a cell wall, chloroplasts and a large vacuole.

items.q: What is the job of the chloroplasts?
c: It controls the cell and contains the genetic material (DNA).
They are where photosynthesis makes food.
It is filled with cell sap and keeps the cell firm.
It is a jelly where most chemical reactions happen.
items.e: Each part of a cell has a job.

items.q: Where is the cytoplasm found: in animal cells, plant cells or both?
items.e: Plant cells have everything animal cells have, plus a cell wall, chloroplasts and a large vacuole.

items.q: Where is the cell membrane found: in animal cells, plant cells or both?
items.e: Plant cells have everything animal cells have, plus a cell wall, chloroplasts and a large vacuole.

items.q: Why do we call the drawings of plant and animal cells in textbooks 'models'?
c: They show the main parts of a typical cell, but real cells vary in shape and size.
They are photographs of one real cell.
They show every part of every cell exactly.
items.e: A model is a simplified way of showing an idea.

items.q: Why do root cells have no chloroplasts?
c: Roots are underground with no light, so they cannot photosynthesise.
items.e: No light, no chloroplasts.

items.q: Which part keeps the shape of a plant cell fixed?
items.e: The cell wall is rigid; it gives shape and support.

items.q: What is a cell?
c: the smallest unit of a living organism
items.e: All living things are made of cells.

items.q: Which part of the cell contains DNA?
items.e: Genetic information.

items.q: Which part do plant cells have that animal cells do not?
items.e: Also chloroplasts and a large vacuole.

items.q: Which part of a cell is where photosynthesis makes food?
items.e: Each part of a cell has a job.

items.q: What is a unicellular organism?
c: a living thing with no cells
a living thing made of just one cell
items.e: Amoeba and bacteria.

items.q: What is the cell wall of a plant made of?
items.e: Strong fibres.

items.q: Which part is partially permeable and controls the movement of substances in and out of the cell?
items.e: The cell wall is fully permeable.

items.q: Why are plant leaves green?
c: Their cells contain chloroplasts with green chlorophyll.
items.e: Chlorophyll absorbs light.

items.q: Which part of a cell is a jelly where most chemical reactions happen?
items.e: Each part of a cell has a job.

items.q: Who first saw and named cells, using a microscope in 1665?
items.e: He looked at cork.

items.q: Which part of the cell contains DNA, the genetic material?
items.e: DNA in the nucleus carries the instructions for the cell.

items.q: This is a plant cell. Which part is labelled E?
items.e: Follow each line to the part it touches.

items.q: A cell is round, has no cell wall and carries oxygen in the blood. What kind of cell is it most likely to be?
c: a bacterium with no genetic material
items.e: A red blood cell is an animal cell.

items.q: Where is the cell wall found: in animal cells, plant cells or both?
items.e: Plant cells have everything animal cells have, plus a cell wall, chloroplasts and a large vacuole.

items.q: A cell has a cell wall and many chloroplasts, and comes from a leaf. What kind of cell is it most likely to be?
c: a bacterium with no genetic material
items.e: Leaf cells make food in their chloroplasts.

items.q: This is a plant cell. Which letter labels the cell wall?
items.e: Follow each line to the part it touches.

items.q: A cell has a cell wall and a long, thin extension that takes in water from the soil. What kind of cell is it most likely to be?
c: a bacterium with no genetic material
items.e: A root hair cell is a plant cell with no chloroplasts.

items.q: This is a plant cell. Which letter labels the vacuole?
items.e: Follow each line to the part it touches.

items.q: This is an animal cell. Which letter labels the cytoplasm?
items.e: Follow each line to the part it touches.

items.q: This is a plant cell. Which part is labelled B?
items.e: Follow each line to the part it touches.

items.q: This is a plant cell. Which letter labels the vacuole?
items.e: Follow each line to the part it touches.

items.q: This is an animal cell. Which letter labels the cell membrane?
items.e: Follow each line to the part it touches.

items.q: A cell is from the inside of a person's cheek and has an irregular shape. What kind of cell is it most likely to be?
c: a bacterium with no genetic material
items.e: Cheek cells have no cell wall, so their shape is not fixed.

items.q: This is a plant cell. Which part is labelled D?
items.e: Follow each line to the part it touches.

items.q: This is a plant cell. Which part is labelled C?
items.e: Follow each line to the part it touches.

items.q: A cell has a nucleus, cytoplasm and a cell membrane but no cell wall. What kind of cell is it most likely to be?
c: a bacterium with no genetic material
items.e: Animal cells have no cell wall.

items.q: This is a plant cell. Which part is labelled B?
items.e: Follow each line to the part it touches.

items.q: A cell has a long tail, a nucleus and no cell wall. What kind of cell is it most likely to be?
c: a bacterium with no genetic material
items.e: A sperm cell is an animal cell.

items.q: A cell has a cell wall, a large central vacuole and chloroplasts. What kind of cell is it most likely to be?
c: a bacterium with no genetic material
items.e: Only plant cells have a cell wall and chloroplasts.

items.q: This is a plant cell. Which letter labels the cytoplasm?
items.e: Follow each line to the part it touches.

items.q: This is an animal cell. Which letter labels the nucleus?
items.e: Follow each line to the part it touches.

items.q: Which organ system breaks down food?
items.e: Mouth to intestines.

items.q: Which level of organisation comes after organ?
items.e: Cells → tissues → organs → organ systems → organisms.

items.q: What is an organ?
c: a group of different tissues working together
items.e: The heart, the stomach.

items.q: Is a leaf a cell, a tissue, an organ, an organ system or an organism?
items.e: Cells → tissues → organs → organ systems → organisms.

items.q: What does multicellular mean?
items.e: Humans, trees, dogs.

items.q: Which specialised cell is large and contains a food store for the growing embryo?
items.e: Specialised cells have features that suit their jobs.

items.q: How is a red blood cell adapted for its job?
c: It has no nucleus and a dimpled shape to carry lots of oxygen.
It has a tail to swim to the egg.
It is long with branches to carry electrical messages.
It is packed with chloroplasts for photosynthesis.
items.e: Specialised cells have features that suit their jobs.

items.q: Is the kidney a cell, a tissue, an organ, an organ system or an organism?
items.e: Cells → tissues → organs → organ systems → organisms.

items.q: Why are some cells called specialised?
c: They have no nucleus at all.
They have special features for a particular job.
items.e: Shape fits job.

items.q: Which level of organisation comes after tissue?
items.e: Cells → tissues → organs → organ systems → organisms.

items.q: What is an organ system?
c: a group of organs working together
items.e: The digestive system.

items.q: Is a goldfish a cell, a tissue, an organ, an organ system or an organism?
items.e: Cells → tissues → organs → organ systems → organisms.

items.q: Which organ system includes the heart and blood vessels?
items.e: It moves blood.

items.q: Is a red blood cell a cell, a tissue, an organ, an organ system or an organism?
items.e: Cells → tissues → organs → organ systems → organisms.

items.q: What is meant by division of labour in a multicellular organism?
c: Cells divide into two all the time.
Different cells are specialised to carry out different jobs.
Only one cell does all the work.
items.e: This makes the organism work efficiently.

items.q: Who first used the word 'cell' after looking at cork under an early microscope?
items.e: Better microscopes later let scientists see the nucleus and other parts.

items.q: Which specialised cell has a long, thin hair to take in water from the soil?
items.e: Specialised cells have features that suit their jobs.

items.q: What is a tissue?
c: a group of similar cells working together
items.e: Muscle tissue.

items.q: Is fat tissue a cell, a tissue, an organ, an organ system or an organism?
items.e: Cells → tissues → organs → organ systems → organisms.

items.q: Which is the correct order, from smallest to largest?
items.e: Cells make tissues; tissues make organs.

items.q: Which part of a light microscope is the part that shines light up through the slide?
items.e: Learn the parts of the microscope.

items.q: A microscope gives a total magnification of ×1500 with a ×15 eyepiece. What is the objective magnification?
items.e: Objective = total ÷ eyepiece = 1500 ÷ 15 = 100.

items.q: What is the fine focusing knob of a light microscope?
c: the lens just above the slide that you choose for low or high power
the flat platform where the slide is placed
the knob that moves the stage a lot to get the image roughly in focus
the knob that makes small changes to sharpen the image
items.e: Learn the parts of the microscope.

items.q: A microscope has a ×5 eyepiece lens and a ×4 objective lens. What is the total magnification?
items.e: Total magnification = eyepiece × objective = 5 × 4 = 20.

items.q: A microscope gives a total magnification of ×200 with a ×5 eyepiece. What is the objective magnification?
items.e: Objective = total ÷ eyepiece = 200 ÷ 5 = 40.

items.q: A microscope has a ×5 eyepiece lens and a ×10 objective lens. What is the total magnification?
items.e: Total magnification = eyepiece × objective = 5 × 10 = 50.

items.q: What is the stage of a light microscope?
c: the knob that moves the stage a lot to get the image roughly in focus
the flat platform where the slide is placed
the knob that makes small changes to sharpen the image
items.e: Learn the parts of the microscope.

items.q: What is the light source (lamp or mirror) of a light microscope?
c: the flat platform where the slide is placed
the knob that makes small changes to sharpen the image
the part that shines light up through the slide
items.e: Learn the parts of the microscope.

items.q: A microscope has a ×10 eyepiece lens and a ×40 objective lens. What is the total magnification?
items.e: Total magnification = eyepiece × objective = 10 × 40 = 400.

items.q: Why should you never use a mirror to reflect direct sunlight into a microscope?
items.e: Safety.

items.q: Why is a stain such as iodine added to an onion cell slide?
c: to make parts of the cells easier to see
items.e: Contrast.

items.q: A microscope gives a total magnification of ×50 with a ×10 objective lens. What is the eyepiece magnification?
items.e: Eyepiece = total ÷ objective = 50 ÷ 10 = 5.

items.q: What is the objective lens of a light microscope?
c: the lens just above the slide that you choose for low or high power
the part that shines light up through the slide
the knob that makes small changes to sharpen the image
items.e: Learn the parts of the microscope.

items.q: What is the coarse focusing knob of a light microscope?
c: the lens just above the slide that you choose for low or high power
the flat platform where the slide is placed
the knob that moves the stage a lot to get the image roughly in focus
items.e: Learn the parts of the microscope.

items.q: A microscope gives a total magnification of ×50 with a ×5 eyepiece. What is the objective magnification?
items.e: Objective = total ÷ eyepiece = 50 ÷ 5 = 10.

items.q: What is the eyepiece lens of a light microscope?
c: the flat platform where the slide is placed
the knob that moves the stage a lot to get the image roughly in focus
the lens just above the slide that you choose for low or high power
items.e: Learn the parts of the microscope.

items.q: A microscope gives a total magnification of ×40 with a ×4 objective lens. What is the eyepiece magnification?
items.e: Eyepiece = total ÷ objective = 40 ÷ 4 = 10.

items.q: Which part of a light microscope is the lens just above the slide that you choose for low or high power?
items.e: Learn the parts of the microscope.

items.q: When focusing a microscope, which objective lens should you start with?
items.e: Find the cells first, then zoom in.

items.q: A cell is 0.01 mm wide. It is viewed at ×40. How wide does it look in the image?
items.e: Image size = real size × magnification = 0.01 × 40 = 0.4 mm.

items.q: Why is the nucleus important when a cell divides?
c: It passes the genetic information (DNA) to the new cells.
items.e: Each new cell needs its own copy of DNA.

items.q: This is a plant cell. Which letter labels the cell membrane?
items.e: Follow each line to the part it touches.

items.q: When focusing under high power, which knob should be used?
c: both knobs as fast as possible
items.e: The coarse knob may crush the slide on high power.

items.q: Which specialised cell has no nucleus and a dimpled shape to carry lots of oxygen?
items.e: Specialised cells have features that suit their jobs.

items.q: Why must a thin, single layer of onion skin be used on a slide?
c: So that light can pass through it and the cells can be seen clearly.
So that it does not need a stain.
items.e: Thick samples block light.

items.q: Why does euglena have both a chloroplast and an eyespot?
c: It can make food in light and swims towards light.
It is a plant cell only.
items.e: A unicellular organism.

items.q: A microscope gives a total magnification of ×60 with a ×4 objective lens. What is the eyepiece magnification?
items.e: Eyepiece = total ÷ objective = 60 ÷ 4 = 15.

items.q: This is a plant cell. Which letter labels the cell wall?
items.e: Follow each line to the part it touches.

items.q: A microscope has a ×15 eyepiece lens and a ×40 objective lens. What is the total magnification?
items.e: Total magnification = eyepiece × objective = 15 × 40 = 600.

items.q: Cells in the small intestine are folded and have tiny projections. What is the most likely reason?
c: to increase the surface area for absorbing digested food
items.e: The shape of a specialised cell suits its job.

items.q: Which specialised cell is long with branches to carry electrical messages?
items.e: Specialised cells have features that suit their jobs.

items.q: What is an amoeba?
c: a unicellular organism that moves and feeds by changing shape
items.e: One cell does everything.

items.q: A cell has a cell membrane, cytoplasm and a nucleus. Which conclusion is correct?
c: It must be an animal cell.
It must be a plant cell.
It is not a living cell.
It could be either a plant or an animal cell; more evidence is needed.
items.e: Both kinds of cell have these parts.

items.e: Follow each line to the part it touches.

A cell is 0.02 mm wide. It is viewed at ×50. How wide does it look in the image?

items.q: A microscope gives a total magnification of ×40 with a ×10 eyepiece. What is the objective magnification?
items.e: Objective = total ÷ eyepiece = 40 ÷ 10 = 4.

items.q: This is a plant cell. Which part is labelled A?
items.e: Follow each line to the part it touches.

items.q: A microscope has a ×5 eyepiece lens and a ×100 objective lens. What is the total magnification?
items.e: Total magnification = eyepiece × objective = 5 × 100 = 500.

items.q: Which specialised cell has a tail to swim to the egg?
items.e: Specialised cells have features that suit their jobs.
